read/order: Dog chases cat. Cat chases dog. The same three words, in another order, say something else. A network that reads text has to keep track of the order.
read/slots: One way is to give every position its own slot: lay the words' embeddings side by side, in order, as one long input, and feed that to a two-layer network.
read/fixed: But a network's input has a fixed size. It must be built for the longest sentence, so a word past the end has nowhere to go.
read/elman: In 1990, Jeffrey Elman's paper, Finding Structure in Time, argued against laying time out in space like this. The network, he wrote, must be given memory.
read/copy: So read one token at a time. After each step, the hidden units' values are copied, and fed back in alongside the next token. Elman called these copies context units.
read/chain: Draw the steps in a row, and the memory passes along it: the hidden state, h. It starts as all zeros, and after each token it holds a summary of everything read so far.
read/name: The same step comes round again at every token, with its output fed back in as input. That is why this is called a recurrent network.
step/t: Zoom in on one step. Number the tokens with t, so this is step t. The memory it starts from is h of t minus one: the hidden state after the token before.
step/x: Its new input is x of t, the embedding of token t.
step/Whh: A matrix of weights, W h h, mixes the old memory. Its two h's say what it connects: hidden to hidden.
step/mem: Here it turns the memory, zero point five and minus zero point five, into zero point five and minus one.
step/Wxh: A second matrix, W x h, input to hidden, brings in the token. It turns zero and one into two and one.
step/b: Add the two results, plus a bias, b: minus one point five and minus zero point five.
step/z: The total is z, the pre-activation, as in a neuron: one, and minus zero point five.
step/tanh: Then tan-aitch squashes each entry into the range between minus one and one: zero point seven six, and minus zero point four six. That is the new memory, h of t.
step/why: Why squash? The memory goes back through W h h at every step. Here that doubles its second entry each time, so without a squash, that entry could keep on growing. tan-aitch keeps every entry between minus one and one.
step/line: All of it in one line: h of t is the tan-aitch of W h h times h of t minus one, plus W x h times x of t, plus b.
loop/loop: To read a whole sentence, run the step in a loop, once per token, each step starting from the memory the last one left.
loop/first: The first step starts from h zero, all zeros, so W h h times it is zero: only the first token counts.
loop/same: Every step uses the same W h h, the same W x h, and the same b. Nothing is added per token, so one network reads three words or three hundred.
loop/order: And order now counts. Run dog chases cat, and cat chases dog, through these same weights, and they end with different memories.
loop/H: Say the memory has capital H numbers, one per hidden unit. W h h turns H numbers into H, so it is H by H.
loop/D: W x h turns a token's D numbers, the size of its embedding, into H, so it is H by D.
loop/bias: And b adds one number to each hidden unit's total: H of them, as many as the memory has.
